These are what are commonly referred to as "deviant thoughts". These are impulsive flashes accompanied by an emotional and adverse response, which is there to make sure you don't do that thing. New mothers often have the deviant thought of throwing their baby from a high height, or drowning it, or any range of thing that would do it harm. This is completely normal, but people have been trained to think that it isn't, that there's something wrong with them. There's not.

There's a tangent of this that says fully engaging those deviant thoughts is healthy, as it lets one fully explore the implications of the act. There's little psychological risk of desiring to engage in those behaviors, as a result of engaging in the thought/fantasy. If you were inclined to then you would, or environmental pressures would guide you towards the act anyways. This logical extensions explains why having an "outlet" for the thoughts is a healthy thing; and by outlet i mean something to help one engage more fully in the hypothetical reality of the deviant thought and it's implications. It's a bit like making a plan for the future.

The unhealthy thing to do is to bottle the emotions/thoughts up or try to push them away. This is because when environmental pressures force you into a situation where you have to engage with the possible reality of the thought, you won't have the cultivated reaction that you would have otherwise formed to deal with it.

There are so many extensions/branches to this concept that it's hard to know where to stop. There's something that probably should be said for too fully engaging in the "fantasy" or healthy/unhealthy redirection of emotional response vs engaging the stressors. Whenever I find myself having "bad" thoughts or urges I have a few methods of dealing with them. The two I use most are using my imagination to follow my thoughts to their logical conclusion and analyzing why I'm having those thoughts, often times I'll use both one after the other. So, for example, you want to punch someone for whatever reason what would probably happen if you punched that person? They might punch you back, they might press charges, they might be knocked out fall and get a head injury or something like that. None of those situations would benefit you in any way or be "good" in general. So the decision has to become "do not do it". Then the second part, why did you have that thought? Maybe the person said or did something to piss you off or maybe it was just a random urge either way once you identify a potential cause (I say potential because, at least for me, I am never certain if I am correct or not unless it's really obvious) you can use that as a building block for how to deal with that thought. Personally I make "rules" that I have no choice but to obey except for very specific circumstances which I determine using a reversed first method. Going back to the earlier example "when would it be 'good' or 'acceptable' or 'necessary' to punch someone?" (I generally don't consider the acceptable option) Once the rule is made it is set in stone so to speak, I occasionally recheck my rules to see if my original conclusions are still valid because new information. Violating the rule is no longer an option. You might ask "Why is it no longer an option?" I used to redo all the thoughts that lead me to that conclusion which reinforces the decision. Alternatively you could ask if any new information has been discovered that is relevant to the decision if the answer is no then the decision stands regardless of your wants at the time. You have to trust that you made a good decision in the past and (since there is no new information that applies) there is no reason to change that decision.

Fast help -

Like when a song gets stuck in your head, and you can only think of the chorus, but if you sing the entire song a couple of time out loud you can help get your brain out of that loop. Hearing it is processed differently in your brain - trying to think it over your bad thoughts isn't as constructive.

Physical pain - when i was younger I would have these bouts of just CRAZY anger. I would just get so mad it was kind of scary because I was a kid and didn't get what was happening. i started collecting those .25 arm bands from the little machines outside the grocery and when I'd get mad i would start walking (ANGRY walking, as a friend put it) and i would snap the shit out of those bands. It would make my wrists throb and kind of ground me, give me something else to focus on. If you do this, MAKE A RULE - never use something that you can't leave around the house/show out in public to ground yourself. A lot of people try to ground themselves using razors or knives and these turn into suicide attempts. You might feel bad at the moment, but its not worth dying over. Seriously. It's temporary. Those bands were great, even the dumb ones, because no one ever got hurt. (Except the bands - I snapped a lot.) If you wouldn't want your grandmother, mom, dad, little brother/sister asking you about it, then you shouldn't be using it. Walking around with a razorblade bracelet isn't edgy (heh) and daring, it makes you look like an emo whiny baby and if you're already feeling bad, why invite that hell?

Exercise (or other physical/mental stressors) - another kind of physical action to give your mind the 'jump' it needs to get to another thought.

NO ONE WANTS TO EXERCISE. Nobody. But sometimes that sluggish feeling you feel isn't just physical, it's mental. First suggestion - make a list of upbeat music you can lose yourself in and pick a small area to walk. I started walking around the block near my house. Don't keep count of how many times you've gone around it, just keep walking until you're tired. Sometimes it takes less time to 'come down' than you think and keeping count can throw you off. Walking gets your juices flowing, oxygen to your brain, I'm not going to pretend everyone knows the science behind it. Walking it out to loud music makes you feel better and you can do it on your lunch break, between classes, hell even on a date - just say you need some air and go walk it out. (Might want to put a timer that last one - they will leave your ass with the whole bill if they think you're ditching them.) Pop those earbuds in and start making laps of the backyard/parking lot/block/office. Don't pay attention to the people around you (beyond making sure you aren't walking into traffic/coworkers/fellow students.). If case anyone asks - pick a story and stick to it. Getting in your 10,000 steps when you can, fitting in your daily exercise, using music to think through a problem - whatever. You don't owe those guys anything so pick a response and give it to everyone. They'll respect you for it.

Long term help -

Cry it out - sometimes you just need to, and that's fine. There is this song that gets me started every time - Feels Like Home - Edwina Hayes DON'T WATCH THIS SHIT RIGHT NOW. It's sad as fuck and then gets happy/sad (Sappy? Had?) The voice is beautiful, the song is beautiful, and it makes you cry. The End. Sometimes I get frustrated, angry, annoyed, and crying it out is helpful to me. I feel better - like letting a big balloon burst. A good long cry can make me feel better for days, not sure why. Fast help -

Meditate it out - sometimes reminding yourself 'This is my brain cycling itself, just like the washing machine - it's temporary and it's moving me to different thought. This is my brain acting weird, and once it's done I can move on to something else'. SAY IT OUT LOUD SO YOU CAN HEAR IT. Focusing on the thoughts just long enough to get the thought out sometimes help. Like when a song gets stuck in your head, and you can only think of the chorus, but if you sing the entire song a couple of time out loud you can help get your brain out of that loop. Hearing it is processed differently in your brain - trying to think it over your bad thoughts isn't as constructive.

Physical pain - when i was younger I would have these bouts of just CRAZY anger. I would just get so mad it was kind of scary because I was a kid and didn't get what was happening. i started collecting those .25 arm bands from the little machines outside the grocery and when I'd get mad i would start walking (ANGRY walking, as a friend put it) and i would snap the shit out of those bands. It would make my wrists throb and kind of ground me, give me something else to focus on. If you do this, MAKE A RULE - never use something that you can't leave around the house/show out in public to ground yourself. A lot of people try to ground themselves using razors or knives and these turn into suicide attempts. You might feel bad at the moment, but its not worth dying over. Seriously. It's temporary. Those bands were great, even the dumb ones, because no one ever got hurt. (Except the bands - I snapped a lot.) If you wouldn't want your grandmother, mom, dad, little brother/sister asking you about it, then you shouldn't be using it. Walking around with a razorblade bracelet isn't edgy (heh) and daring, it makes you look like an emo whiny baby and if you're already feeling bad, why invite that hell?

First suggestion - make a list of upbeat music you can lose yourself in and pick a small area to walk. I started walking around the block near my house. Don't keep count of how many times you've gone around it, just keep walking until you're tired. Sometimes it takes less time to 'come down' than you think and keeping count can throw you off. Walking gets your juices flowing, oxygen to your brain, I'm not going to pretend everyone knows the science behind it. Walking it out to loud music makes you feel better and you can do it on your lunch break, between classes, hell even on a date - just say you need some air and go walk it out. (Might want to put a timer that last one - they will leave your ass with the whole bill if they think you're ditching them.) Getting in your 10,000 steps when you can, fitting in your daily exercise, using music to think through a problem - whatever. You don't owe those guys anything so pick a response and give it to everyone. They'll respect you for it.
